lesson-intro.text: Canal towns are full of old stone bridges. The still water turns every arch into a ring. Watch it take shape, then cross over to your own page.

waterline.text: Start with the waterline: one long level line straight across.

bridge.text: The bridge's two ends stand on it, joined by a humped top. A second hump runs just below.

middle-arch.text: In the middle, a tall round arch with a second one inside. Two short lines at the top make the wedge.

middle-stones.text: Three more lines down each side split the ring into stones. Each points at the middle.

side-arches.text: Then a smaller arch on each side, doubled the same way.

left-stones.text: The left ring gets five lines: one at the top, then two down each side.

right-stones.text: Five more on the right ring, placed the same way.

quays.text: A brick wall along each bank: a flat top, a band just under it, and a straight outer end.

left-house.text: A small house stands on the left bank: two sides, a sloping roof and one window.

right-house.text: The right house matches it, its roof sloping the other way.

trees.text: A tall pointed tree on the left bank. On the right, a round one on a short trunk.

water.text: Now the canal: down from the waterline's left end, across the bottom and back up.

mirror-arches.text: In the water each arch shows again, upside down. Its rings close into circles.

reflection.text: Carry the bridge's ends down into the water. Then its mirror: level, a dip, level again.

ripples.text: Three pairs of short level lines make ripples.

blue.text: Blue for the water, inside the mirrored arches too, and both windows.

cream-gray.text: Cream for the bands along the top, the stones and the reflection. Gray for the mirrored rings.

yellow.text: Yellow for the bridge and the left house.

red-pink.text: Red for the brick walls and the left roof. Pink for their reflections.

orange-brown.text: Orange for the right house, brown for its roof and trunk. Dark green and green for the trees.

lesson-outro.text: Your bridge is standing, and so is its twin in the water. Which one would you walk across?
